newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's "Black Widow" gets life behind bars.
newsitem.headline: Austria's "Black Widow" gets life behind bars.

text.p: An Austrian court on Friday sentenced "Black Widow' Elfriede Blauensteiner to life imprisonment for the murder of a pensioner in one of the most notorious trials in the country's history.

The court in Krems, 50 km (30 miles) west of Vienna, found Blauensteiner, 66, guilty of poisoning 77-year-old Alois Pichler with fatal doses of medication. The jury reached its verdict at three a.m.(0200 GMT) after 12 hours of deliberation.

Blauensteiner, in a black suit and cream blouse, remained composed, muttering and looking at her watch impatiently as the verdict was read out. Asked if she understood the sentence she said with defiance: "I understand perfectly".
The eight-person jury said Blauensteiner's "pure greed" justified the heavy sentence, noting her "malicious actions did not give the victim any chance to defend himself".
Blauensteiner's former lawyer Harald Schmidt was sentenced to seven years in jail for being an accomplice to grevious bodily harm and falsifying Pichler's will.
The two have said they may appeal the verdict.
Although Blauensteiner was charged with only one murder, police are still investigating other deaths possibly linked to the blonde bespectacled pensioner.

The case has all the elements of a Hollywood thriller. Blauensteiner is accused of placing advertisements in newspapers to meet rich, elderly men, allegedly poisoning her victims and then gambling away the money she was left in their wills.
Blauensteiner arrived last month for the start of the high-profile trial clutching a golden crucifix, claiming it was intended to protect her from vampires.
The matronly-looking woman said she enjoyed nursing pensioners through the autumn of their years and it was a coincidence that some of her patients subsequently died.

She was arrested in January last year, suspected of a murder spree spanning over a decade. Police have exhumed the corpses of three pensioners nursed by Blauensteiner, although one was too decomposed for forensic examination.
Police said she confessed to five murders, including that of her late husband Rudolf, during the initial investigation but later withdrew the confession.

She was charged with giving Pichler anti-depressants and diabetes medicine, leaving him in a room with the windows open all night and then putting him under a hot shower, which caused his fatal heart attack.

Doctors said a lethal dose of medicine was found in the body of Pichler, a widower and postal worker from Lower Austria. He died in late 1995, just five weeks after he met Blauensteiner through a newspaper advertisement.
She admitted the wealth of prospective patients who replied to her advertisements was a definite factor in her choice. Pichler had a house with a garden and a healthy bank balance.
